system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2178-06-07 18:01:00 to 2178-06-10 17:40:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted with a complicated urinary tract infection due to Pseudomonas aeruginosa, requiring IV cefepime. He also developed Candida parapsilosis in his urine, treated with fluconazole. His hospital course was complicated by severe constipation, managed with repeated MoviPrep and bowel regimen adjustments, and tremors likely due to infection-related myoclonus, leading to discontinuation of duloxetine and initiation of mirtazapine for depression. He experienced transient hypoxia from atelectasis, improved with incentive spirometry, and had a facial rash ruled negative for HSV and VZV. A PICC line was placed for outpatient antibiotic completion. He was discharged to extended care on IV antibiotics, antifungal, and optimized medications for heart failure, constipation, and mood, with plans for urology and primary care follow-up.
problems: Infection and inflammatory reaction due to indwelling urinary catheter
Urinary tract infection, site not specified
Diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled
Pseudomonas infection in conditions classified elsewhere and of unspecified site
Hypertrophy (benign) of prostate without urinary obstruction and other lower urinary tract symptom (LUTS)
Rash and other nonspecific skin eruption
Unspecified disorder of kidney and ureter
Urinary catheterization as the cause of abnormal reaction of patient, or of later complication, without mention of misadventure at time of procedure

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___. I’m Dr. ___. You were brought in today because of some facial twitching and lower abdominal pain. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve had some belly pain for about a week, off and on. The twitching… I think that’s been happening for months, but the staff just noticed it today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any fever, chills, or feeling unwell?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, not really. I just haven’t felt like eating much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Your urine test showed a lot of bacteria and white blood cells, which suggests a urinary tract infection. We also gave you some antibiotics in the ER—cefepime—to cover possible resistant organisms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I get these infections a lot because of my catheter. Is that why I’m here?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. While you often have bacteria in your urine without symptoms, this time you developed confusion and twitching, which suggests the infection is affecting your brain—what we call delirium. That’s why we’re treating it aggressively.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I’ve been a bit foggy. I didn’t know that was from the infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s common in older patients with UTIs, especially with a catheter. We’ve started you on IV antibiotics and will monitor your mental status closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need to stay long?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll need a few days. We’re waiting for the urine culture to confirm which bacteria is causing this, and we may adjust antibiotics based on that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood cultures came back negative so far, which is good—no bloodstream infection. But your urine culture grew Klebsiella pneumoniae, a resistant strain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, but we caught it early. The cefepime you were on wasn’t the best choice for this bug, so we’re switching to imipenem, a stronger antibiotic, through your IV.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be on that the whole time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give it in the hospital for now, then switch you to daily injections of ertapenem for 10 more days after discharge. You’ll get those at the extended care facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a CT scan of your head today to check for any new strokes or bleeding, since you had twitching and confusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No new problems. You have a small old stroke in the basal ganglia, which we’ve seen before, and a stable benign brain lesion. Nothing new or dangerous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to hear. I was worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We are too, but it looks like your confusion and jerking were due to the infection. As the antibiotics work, you’re already more alert.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are improving. White blood cell count is down, kidney function is better. The infection is responding well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I feel a bit clearer in my head.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your delirium is lifting. We also noticed a red rash in your groin today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s been a bit sore. Is it serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It looks like a fungal infection—candidiasis—common in skin folds, especially with incontinence. We’ll start a cream, ketoconazole, twice a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll use it as directed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did another chest X-ray today because your oxygen level dipped a bit. It shows some atelectasis—collapsed lung areas—likely from shallow breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at all. It’s common in hospitalized patients. We’ll encourage deep breathing and you should improve quickly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your catheter was changed yesterday. It’s important to do that regularly—every few weeks—to reduce infection risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know. I’ve refused the suprapubic one before, but this one works okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s fine. As long as we keep it clean and change it on schedule, we can prevent many infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your infection is under control. You’re more alert, labs are better, and you’re ready to be discharged today to the extended care facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What about the antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get daily ertapenem injections for 10 more days. Also, keep using the ketoconazole cream for the groin rash until it clears.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my regular meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All the same—no changes. Just those two new additions. And remember, check for UTI symptoms like fever or worsening confusion—don’t treat just based on a urine test alone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll follow up with your care team. Take care, Mr. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Your daughter will be contacted to coordinate your transfer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, she’s expecting the call.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also confirmed your DNR/DNI status—no resuscitation or intubation if needed. That’s still correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I don’t want aggressive measures.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Noted. We’ll make sure that’s documented in your records.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your kidney mass. It’s still stable, and we’ll continue monitoring it with your urologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m not ready for treatment. Just keep watching it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Understood. We’ll follow up as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Get some rest, and we’ll get you moved soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send all instructions to the facility. They’ll continue your care smoothly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the goal. Keep up the progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Someone will be in shortly to help you get ready for transfer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted with a symptomatic urinary tract infection caused by multidrug-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae, complicated by acute delirium and myoclonic jerks. He was started on cefepime, which was later changed to imipenem based on culture results. His mental status improved rapidly with appropriate antibiotic therapy. A groin rash was diagnosed as candidiasis and treated with topical ketoconazole. His foley catheter was exchanged to reduce infection risk. He completed a course of IV antibiotics and was discharged to extended care for 10 days of daily ertapenem injections. His chronic conditions, including diastolic heart failure, benign prostatic hypertrophy, and a right renal mass, remained stable. Blood cultures remained negative, and imaging showed no new acute findings.
